name: Monitoring And Alerting Best Practices
description: This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building monitoring and alerting — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary monitoring and alerting tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.
content:
This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building monitoring and alerting — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary monitoring and alerting tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Re-check edge cases relevant to monitoring and alerting (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
2. Validate monitoring and alerting outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
3. Keep monitoring and alerting changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
4. When multiple monitoring and alerting strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
5. Surface known limitations of a chosen monitoring and alerting approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
6. Prefer explicit, readable monitoring and alerting solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
7. Check that monitoring and alerting terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
8. Measure before optimizing any monitoring and alerting bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of monitoring and alerting correctness.
- Do not silently drop monitoring and alerting edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Do not skip documenting monitoring and alerting assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Do not apply generic monitoring and alerting advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for monitoring and alerting, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
